questions.question: Why is Poseidon typically cheaper than SHA-256 inside SNARK circuits?
options: It is built from field additions/multiplications that map directly to circuit constraints
It is computed with fewer CPU instructions than SHA-256 on all platforms
It is a keyed hash so it avoids preimage attacks automatically
It outputs fewer bits so it is always faster to verify
questions.explanation: SNARKs work natively over a field, so arithmetic operations are much cheaper than bit-level emulation of SHA-256.

questions.question: In a sponge hash, what is the main purpose of the capacity part of the state?
options: It provides a hidden buffer that contributes to security against collisions/preimages
It stores the final output so the rate can be reused for absorbing
It makes the hash deterministic by holding the random seed
It ensures the hash output is always uniformly distributed in bytes
questions.explanation: Capacity is the part not directly overwritten by input; it drives the sponge’s security level.

questions.question: What is the defining difference between full rounds and partial rounds in Poseidon?
options: Full rounds apply the S-box to every state word; partial rounds apply it to only one word
Full rounds use an MDS matrix; partial rounds do not mix the state at all
Full rounds use exponentiation; partial rounds use only additions
Full rounds are optional and can be skipped if inputs are small
questions.explanation: Partial rounds keep the linear mixing but reduce S-box applications to one word per round to save constraints.

questions.question: Why should the S-box exponent α satisfy gcd(α, p−1) = 1 in a prime field F_p?
options: So the map x ↦ x^α is a permutation of the field (invertible nonlinearity)
So x ↦ x^α becomes linear and easier to analyze for security
So the MDS matrix is guaranteed to be invertible
So the round constants do not need to be generated from a seed
questions.explanation: If α is coprime to p−1, exponentiation is bijective on nonzero elements (and 0 maps to 0), making it invertible.

questions.question: What is the main role of the MDS matrix in Poseidon?
options: Diffusion: make each output word depend on all input words after a few rounds
Nonlinearity: provide the only source of confusion in the permutation
Authentication: prevent an attacker from modifying inputs undetected
Compression: reduce the number of field elements in the state
questions.explanation: The MDS layer is linear but ensures changes spread quickly across the entire state.

questions.question: What can go wrong if you hash variable-length inputs with implicit zero padding and no length separation?
options: Trivial collisions like hash([x]) == hash([x, 0]) for many x
The hash becomes keyed without you noticing
The MDS matrix stops being invertible
The field modulus p changes during hashing
questions.explanation: If missing inputs are treated as zeros, multiple different-length inputs can absorb to the same state before permutation.

questions.question: What is domain separation used for in hash-based protocols?
options: To ensure hashes of different object types (leaf vs node, commitment vs nullifier) cannot collide across types
To increase the output size so collisions become impossible
To allow hashing of integers without reducing mod p
To avoid having to choose round constants for Poseidon
questions.explanation: A domain tag effectively creates independent hash functions for different contexts using the same primitive.

questions.question: Two systems use the same field and round counts but different round constants. What happens?
options: They compute different hashes; interoperability breaks (proofs/roots won’t match)
They compute the same hashes because the MDS matrix dominates the result
They become vulnerable only to length-extension attacks, but outputs still match
They can be made compatible by swapping endianness of inputs
questions.explanation: Round constants are part of the hash definition. Different constants mean a different permutation and different outputs.
